name: Wendy Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself and how you came to line work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a bank teller for eighteen years, same branch on the high street, until they closed it because everyone banks on their phone now. I took the redundancy money, which is a big part of our savings, and at 41 I signed up for the line apprenticeship at the electricity company because I wanted something that couldn't be done from a phone. I'm in my second year. My husband Dev drives a lorry for a building supplier, and we've got Asha, who's thirteen, and Kiran, who's ten.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Our crew mostly connects new houses on the estates going up on the edge of town, places like Oakfield, where they're putting up three hundred homes. So it's digging trenches, setting poles, fitting meters and running the service lines to each house, with Mick, our crew leader, checking everything I do twice. I'm careful, I'm slow, and I write everything in a little notebook because I don't trust myself yet. I like that it's real, that at the end of the day a family can switch the kettle on. What wears me out is my back, and being told off in front of the younger ones, which I took a lot more gracefully at 25 than I do at 43.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, everyone can calm down now. At work I'd probably not say much at all, because Mick and the lads don't talk about this stuff. If my sister brought it up at Sunday lunch, I'd say I never believed the half of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, properly relieved. I already lost one job to machines and I picked this one so I wouldn't have to go through that again. If nothing changes, I can just learn my trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, really. I'd carry on with the apprenticeship, and we'd keep putting money aside every month the way we do. I'd keep my notebook and keep asking Mick stupid questions until they stop being stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AI Plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved. Like when the doctor rings and says the test was fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about losing the bank job. What was that like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They didn't close it overnight. First they cut the counter hours, then they put in machines in the lobby, then they moved two of us to other branches, and then one Tuesday the area manager came in with an envelope. I'd known since the machines went in, really. I just didn't want to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I don't want to. Kiran uses something for his homework and I've told him he still has to write it in his own hand. I'm not against it for other people, I just don't trust a thing that sounds that sure of itself.

S0.say: She'd say everyone can calm down now, and wouldn't talk about it much at work. At Sunday lunch she'd say she never believed the half of it.
S0.think: She'd be properly relieved, because she already lost a bank job to machines and chose line work to avoid that happening again. Nothing changing means she can learn her trade.
S0.do: Carries on with the apprenticeship and keeps saving each month as now. Keeps her notebook and keeps asking her crew leader questions until she knows the work.
S0.feel: Relieved, like getting good news from the doctor.
S0.quote: Then one Tuesday the area manager came in with an envelope.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy's earlier redundancy from a bank is the lens for everything. Her choice of line work was deliberately a choice of safety. She avoids AI tools and is wary of anything that sounds too sure of itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame for people, but that's how things go, and you have to keep up. At work I'd say we're lucky we work with our hands. I wouldn't post anything, I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it brings back the bank, and I don't like it. The machines came in slowly there too, one task at a time, and everyone said most people would still have work, which was true, just not us. I think our jobs are safer, but I don't fully believe it any more when someone says that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get qualified as quickly as I can, because a qualified lineworker is harder to let go than an apprentice. We'd stop the extra holiday this year and put that money in savings instead. If the company made us use some new tablet or program, I'd do the training, but I wouldn't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing Steady Disruption?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a little voice saying 'here we go again'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a qualified lineworker is harder to let go. Who else at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the office girls who do the job scheduling. That's exactly the kind of thing that went first at the bank, the planning and the forms. Mick's wife, Carol, does that job, and I wouldn't want to be her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Dev's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev drives, and I've read about lorries driving themselves, though I've never seen one. He just laughs and says he'll believe it when one can reverse into our supplier's yard, because it's a nightmare. I hope he's right, but I said the same about the bank.

S1.say: She'd say it's a shame but that's how things go and you have to keep up. At work she'd say they're lucky to work with their hands, and she'd post nothing.
S1.think: It brings back the bank, where machines came in one task at a time and people were told most would still have work. She thinks line work is safer but no longer fully trusts that.
S1.do: Gets qualified as fast as she can, since an apprentice is easier to let go. Skips the extra holiday this year to save the money, and does any required training without seeking it out.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a little voice saying 'here we go again'.
S1.quote: Everyone said most people would still have work, which was true, just not us.
S1.fieldNote: She takes the card's own reassurance and turns it against itself, from experience. She worries about the schedulers in the office and her husband's driving job more than her own trench work. She acts by saving and keeping her head down, not by learning new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say something like, well, nobody saw that coming, and we'll have to see what the government does. I'm not one for protests. I'd say it calmly, but people who know me would see I wasn't calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be in a state. Two years means I'm not even qualified, Dev's job could go too, and I'd be 45 and losing a job to machines for the second time. We've got savings, but savings run out, and then what, two of us looking for work against robots?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd sit down with Dev and go through every bill, and cut everything that isn't the mortgage, food and the kids. No holidays, no new car, Asha's dance classes on hold if we have to. I'd keep turning up to work every day until they tell me not to, because I'm not walking away from a paycheque early. And I'd ring my brother, who's an accountant, to ask what we should do with the redundancy money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick to my stomach. Like the morning of the envelope, but for the whole country.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the two-year timing make it different from the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is barely enough to notice it's happening. At the bank I had a good few years of watching the machines creep in, and even that wasn't enough to get ready. Two years, I'd just be holding on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep turning up until they tell you not to. What would you tell Asha and Kiran?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much at first, they're kids. Asha would notice, though, because she notices when I go quiet. I'd tell her Mum's job might change, and that we'll be all right, and I'd try to believe it while I said it.

S2.say: She'd say nobody saw it coming and they'll have to see what the government does. She isn't one for protests and would sound calm, though people close to her would see she wasn't.
S2.think: She'd be in a state: not yet qualified, Dev's driving job also at risk, and facing a second job loss to machines at 45. Savings run out, and then they'd be two people competing with robots.
S2.do: Goes through every bill with Dev in the first week and cuts everything but the mortgage, food and the kids, including holidays and possibly Asha's dance classes. Keeps turning up to work and asks her accountant brother what to do with the redundancy money.
S2.feel: Sick to her stomach, like the morning of the redundancy envelope but for the whole country.
S2.quote: Like the morning of the envelope, but for the whole country.
S2.fieldNote: Strong savings don't calm her, because she's been through a job loss and knows how fast things go. Her instinct is to cut spending and hold on, not to campaign or retrain. Her brother is the person she'd turn to for advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't much, but it's something, and everyone should get their house in order. At work I'd say we should ask the company what its plans are. I'd say it once, politely, and probably not again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gets me qualified with a couple of years of proper wages. That helps. But then I'm 48 with a trade that's gone, and I've already done the starting-over thing once and I don't know if I have it in me twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, and I'd take every bit of overtime going to build up the savings. Dev and I would start overpaying the mortgage so it's smaller by the time it hits. I'd keep an eye out for jobs that still need a person in the room, like care work maybe, but I wouldn't jump until I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like watching a wave come in from a long way off and not being able to move your feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned care work. Is that something you'd really consider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. My mum was in a care home at the end and the staff were wonderful and paid nothing. I don't know if I'd be good at it, and it would be a big pay cut, but people will always want a person holding their hand, won't they? Or I hope so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't jump until you had to. If you could see it coming, why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I jumped once already and landed somewhere I'm still not good at. Every time you start again you're the slowest person in the room, and I'm tired of being that person. So I'd rather squeeze every year out of this one first.

S3.say: She'd say five years isn't much but it's something, and people should get their house in order. At work she'd ask, once and politely, what the company's plans are.
S3.think: She thinks five years gets her qualified with a couple of years of proper wages, but at 48 she'd have a trade that's gone. She doubts she has a second restart in her.
S3.do: Qualifies, takes every bit of overtime to build savings, and overpays the mortgage with Dev. Keeps an eye on jobs that still need a person, such as care work, but doesn't move until she must.
S3.feel: Anxious, like watching a distant wave and not being able to move.
S3.quote: Every time you start again you're the slowest person in the room, and I'm tired of being that person.
S3.fieldNote: I named the gap between seeing it coming and waiting, and she explained it with real weariness about being the beginner again. Care work is a hope rooted in her mother's last years. She'd build cash rather than move early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and lots can happen. I'd tell people not to panic and to plan. At work I'd say it'll be after most of us are gone anyway, though that's not really true for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'd get eight good years as a lineworker and be 53. That's a long way from the bank, and a long way from the edge. I could get the mortgage down a lot by then, and the kids would be grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, work, save and pay the mortgage down hard. Maybe around year six or seven, I'd look at what jobs are still around and take a course in something, if the company paid for it. I'd tell Asha to think about something with people, like nursing, instead of something on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's in the background. Ten years is long enough that I could put it in a drawer most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'after most of us are gone' isn't really true for you. Why say it at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what you say at work, isn't it? Mick and the lads are mostly in their fifties, so for them it's nearly true. For me, I'd keep my mouth shut and do my sums at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk to Asha about nursing? She's thirteen.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gently. She likes science and she's kind, so it's not mad. But I'd not push, my mum pushed me into the bank and look how that turned out.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a long time and people should plan rather than panic. At work she'd say it will come after most of them have retired, though that isn't true for her.
S4.think: She thinks ten years gives her eight good years as a lineworker, a much smaller mortgage and grown kids by 53. That feels a long way from the edge.
S4.do: Qualifies, works, saves and pays the mortgage down hard. Around year six or seven looks for a company-paid course in work that's still around, and gently steers Asha towards a people-focused job like nursing.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background, something she could put in a drawer most days.
S4.quote: Mick and the lads are mostly in their fifties, so for them it's nearly true. For me, I'd keep my mouth shut and do my sums at home.
S4.fieldNote: The clearest gap between what she'd say at work and what she thinks appears here. Ten years lets her relax enough to plan slowly, mainly through the mortgage. She'd advise her daughter gently, remembering being pushed into banking herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be losing a job to machines twice in five years, and Dev's too, maybe. What would help is a bit of notice and honesty from the company, not an envelope on a Tuesday, and some proper help finding the next thing, with someone who knows the local jobs, not a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about how tired people get. Everyone talks about retraining like it's easy. I did it at 41 and it's the hardest thing I've ever done, and I'd want people deciding these things to know that.

headlineQuote: I'd known since the machines went in, really. I just didn't want to know.
portrait: Wendy Gupta is a 43-year-old second-year apprentice who connects new housing estates for a large electricity company, after eighteen years as a bank teller whose branch closed. Her redundancy money is a big part of a solid cushion, and she chose line work because it couldn't be done from a phone. She never uses AI and is wary of anything that sounds too sure of itself. Calm in the plateau, she grows uneasy in steady change because it echoes the bank, and alarmed when AGI arrives in two years and threatens her and her lorry-driver husband. With more warning she saves hard and pays down the mortgage, but admits she's too tired of being the beginner to jump early.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd lose a job to machines for the second time in five years, possibly alongside her husband.
whatWouldHelp: Notice and honesty from the company instead of a sudden envelope, plus in-person help from someone who knows the local jobs.
